strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: understanding when MoE models are suitable for expert offloading on memory-constrained devices.

Introduces two clearly defined metrics for local routing consistency: SRP, a parameter-free segment-level routing metric, and SCH, a cache-size-constrained segment cache hit-rate metric, including formal derivations and proofs.
Conducts an extensive empirical study across 20 MoE LLMs spanning 3B–57B parameters and diverse architectures, domains, layer positions, and expert specializations.

Provides actionable findings, such as the association between high local routing consistency and MoE-on-every-layer/no-shared-expert designs, the greater role of domain specialization over vocabulary specialization, and the observation that cache sizes around 2x active experts show diminishing returns in hit rate.

Reproducibility is relatively strong: deterministic data construction, plans to release code and corpus, bootstrap confidence intervals for key results, and explicit ethics/reproducibility statements.
The paper is generally well organized, with useful appendices covering additional analyses, layer-wise/expert-wise results, and base vs. post-trained comparisons.
weaknesses: The central practical claims about expert-offloading efficiency and inference speed are not directly validated by end-to-end deployment experiments measuring latency, throughput, memory traffic, or model quality under segment caching.

SCH is an oracle segment-level upper bound that assumes future segment information and no cache-switching cost; its correlation with online cache algorithms does not fully establish that the proposed metrics translate into real system gains, especially during autoregressive decoding.

Architecture conclusions are largely correlational and may be confounded by model size, training data, tokenizer, MoE layer placement, active-parameter ratio, and model family; the paper does not provide controlled architecture ablations.

The metrics themselves are technically straightforward extensions of existing locality/cache-hit ideas, and the paper does not propose a new router, caching algorithm, or system that improves offloading.
The experiments use fixed 512-token input sequences, which mainly exercise prefilling/parallel token processing, despite the paper motivating the problem through decoding-time expert offloading.
The claim that cache size around 2x active experts balances effectiveness and efficiency is supported only by SCH turning points, not by measured efficiency, so it is stronger than the evidence.
Domain- and vocabulary-specialization analyses rely on correlations and do not establish causal contribution to local routing consistency.

strengths: Empirical breadth: analyzes 20 MoE-based LLMs across diverse architectures, sizes, and domains, which is a substantial data-collection effort.
Proposes two intuitive metrics, SRP and SCH, and provides an extensive appendix with per-layer, per-expert, domain-wise, and position-wise analyses.
Attempts to connect local routing consistency to practical expert offloading by correlating SCH with common cache algorithms.
Reproducibility effort is partially addressed with promises to release code and the sampled corpus, plus deterministic experiment configuration.
The topic is relevant to efficient MoE inference and edge deployment, and the paper identifies potentially useful architectural correlates such as MoE-every-layer and shared-expert design.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the observation that expert routing exhibits locality and benefits caching is already known in prior offloading work; SRP and SCH are relatively straightforward F1/threshold and top-k cache hit-rate measures rather than fundamentally new methodology.

Technical soundness issues: the group-level SRP formulation is not clearly correct. Maximizing aggregate F1 across experts is not separable into independent per-expert thresholds, yet the paper states per-expert alpha_e^m and Equation 6 appears malformed/ambiguous. A rigorous group-level proof is missing.

Metrics are confounded by load imbalance and always-active experts. High SRP can simply reflect a few globally dominant experts rather than local routing consistency, and the paper only partially mitigates this through separate load-balance discussion.

Evaluation lacks end-to-end validation. There is no measurement of actual offloading latency, throughput, memory traffic, or downstream model quality; SCH is only correlated with cache hit rates, not with real system performance.

Causal architecture claims are overclaimed. The finding that MoE-every-layer and no-shared-expert models have highest consistency is correlational and uncontrolled; models differ in size, expert count, top-k, training data, tokenizer, and other factors.

The cache-size recommendation of approximately 2x active experts is weakly justified. It is based mainly on turning points for one model group and lacks a cost model or real latency/bandwidth tradeoff analysis.
Experimental scope is limited to 512-token sequences, so long-context decoding and topic shifts—the motivating scenario for expert offloading—are not directly tested.

Baselines are missing: no comparison against alternative locality metrics (e.g., token-to-token expert overlap, reuse distance, entropy) or against existing offloading heuristics beyond basic LRU/LFU/fixed-cache correlations.

Clarity and presentation issues: SRP values are inconsistently reported as decimals in figures and percentages in tables, several equations/formatting are unclear, and some metric definitions lack precise scale and aggregation details.
The paper's practical significance remains indirect: it provides diagnostic metrics but does not demonstrate that optimizing for SRP/SCH actually improves real expert-offloading deployment.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practical problem: understanding when MoE models are amenable to expert offloading and caching.
It proposes two clear, well-motivated metrics, SRP and SCH, that quantify local routing consistency at both expert and model levels.
The empirical study is broad, covering 20 MoE LLMs across different sizes and architectures, with multiple domains and segment lengths.
The analysis yields actionable architectural insights, such as the association between MoE-every-layer/no-shared-expert designs and higher local routing consistency.
The paper connects SRP and SCH to real cache algorithms (LRU, LFU, fixed) and provides correlations supporting the practical relevance of the metrics.
The writing is generally clear, and the authors provide detailed appendices, reproducibility statements, and plans to release code/data.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily a measurement/analysis study; the metrics are intuitive and the main novelty lies in systematic empirical characterization rather than new algorithms or systems.
There is no end-to-end validation with an actual expert-offloading system, so the practical gains from the proposed metrics (latency, throughput, energy) remain unquantified.

Architectural conclusions (e.g., MoE on every layer, no shared experts) are largely correlational and may be confounded by model family, training data, router design, and other factors; causal claims are not established.
The claim that domain-specialized experts contribute more to local routing consistency than vocabulary-specialized experts is supported mainly by correlations without intervention or ablation.
The recommendation of cache size ~2x active experts is derived from oracle-based SCH turning points and may not directly translate to real cache management under latency/cost constraints.
The evaluation uses a fixed corpus of 512-token sequences; longer contexts and decoding-time dynamics, which are central to offloading, are not directly studied.
The paper lacks rigorous statistical testing or controls for the architecture comparisons; many conclusions rely on visual grouping and relative patterns.
Baselines or comparisons to existing locality/offloading heuristics are limited, making it harder to assess the added value of SRP and SCH over prior observations.

strengths: Addresses an important and understudied problem: how local routing consistency of MoE LLMs affects expert offloading efficiency and deployment on memory-constrained devices.

Provides two clear, formally defined metrics: SRP for parameter-free expert/group-level segment routing consistency, and SCH for cache-hit behavior under a hard cache-size limit; SRP includes formal proofs and is well motivated.

Conducts a broad empirical study across 20 MoE LLMs (3B–54B parameters) covering diverse architectures, multiple domains, layer/expert analyses, base vs. post-trained comparisons, and confidence intervals.

Uses toy-model ablations to provide more controlled evidence for factors such as local load balance, shared experts, expert combination space, and dense-layer interleaving, beyond simple cross-model correlations.

Offers several actionable insights for MoE design and offloading: local routing consistency vs. local load balance trade-off, coexistence with global load balance, domain specialization mattering more than vocabulary specialization, and a cache ratio around 2x active experts.
Reproducibility is addressed with deterministic corpus construction, planned code/data release, and an ethics statement.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core metrics are relatively straightforward adaptations of F1 and cache hit rate, and the paper does not propose a new routing, training, or offloading algorithm/system.

Practical validation of the expert-offloading claims is incomplete: SCH is an oracle metric, and the absolute gap between SCH and LRU/LFU hit rates is large at moderate cache sizes (e.g., Table 4), somewhat contradicting the claim that practical cache algorithms can approach SCH; the toy throughput correlations in Appendix F are weak.

Main experiments use fixed 512-token sequences and largely prefilling/base-model routing behavior; real expert offloading is especially sensitive to autoregressive decoding, long-context topic shifts, and system-level latency/throughput, which are not systematically evaluated on real large MoE models.

SRP can be confounded by load imbalance and degenerate routing: high SRP may reflect a few experts being activated almost constantly rather than context-predictable local consistency. The paper discusses this trade-off but does not fully disentangle the two phenomena.

Toy-model conclusions are useful but limited: the models are small, short-trained, and some real-model results (e.g., Phi/GRIN) already contradict stated design rules, so the architectural insights may not scale cleanly.

The recommendation of a cache size around 2x active experts is derived mainly from turning points for one model group and is less clearly supported for other groups; the general claim may be overbroad.

Some claims are stronger than the presented evidence, especially regarding practical cache algorithms approaching SCH and the broad deployment implications, which are not fully demonstrated with end-to-end real-system experiments.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: efficient expert offloading for memory-constrained MoE LLM deployment.
Proposes two quantitative metrics, SRP and SCH, with formal definitions and proofs to characterize local routing consistency.
Conducts a broad empirical study over 20 MoE LLMs spanning different sizes and architectures, plus controlled toy models.
Provides useful observations, such as correlation between SCH and LRU/LFU cache hit rates, and distinctions between domain and vocabulary expert specialization.
Includes a reproducibility statement and promises code/corpus release.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: SRP and SCH are post-hoc diagnostic/oracle metrics rather than new offloading algorithms or architecture designs; the main contribution is measurement and analysis.

The central practical claim that cache size around 2x active experts balances effectiveness and efficiency is not well supported: only Group 1 models show SCH turning points, while Groups 2-4 grow roughly linearly, so the claim for 'most models' is overstated.

Evaluation lacks end-to-end wall-clock throughput/latency for the 20 real models under actual expert offloading; the toy-model throughput correlations in Appendix F are weak and do not convincingly establish practical impact.

Causal claims about shared experts, load balance, and expert combination space are confounded by other architectural/training choices, and toy-model ablations are limited in scale and do not report sufficient variance/robustness.
'Global load balance' coexisting with local routing consistency is not rigorously measured; using overall activation-frequency SD does not adequately capture domain/context-level balance.

The group-level SRP can be inflated by allowing unlimited expert activation, and the supplementary size ratio does not fully resolve comparability across models with different expert counts/activation patterns.

SCH is an oracle based on future activation frequency, but the paper does not demonstrate that this signal is easily learnable in practice; the gap to clairvoyant optimal is nontrivial (e.g., 90.55 vs 100 at rho=2).

Presentation and positioning issues: several conclusions are stronger than the evidence, terminology is occasionally imprecise, and the paper does not sufficiently compare against existing locality/cache metrics for MoE routing.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study across 20 MoE LLMs spanning diverse architectures and scales, plus controlled toy models, providing broad evidence for the proposed analyses.

Introduces two well-motivated metrics, SRP and SCH, with formal definitions and proofs; SRP enables parameter-free expert-level analysis, while SCH explicitly accounts for cache size limits relevant to expert offloading.

Extensive analyses across domains, layers, and experts yield useful practical insights: trade-offs with local load balance, negative association with shared experts, importance of expert combination space, and the role of domain versus vocabulary specialization.
The paper has clear relevance to memory-efficient MoE deployment and offers actionable guidance, such as cache sizes around 2x active experts for models with high local routing consistency.
Writing is clear, reproducibility is supported by deterministic setup and promises of code/data release, and ethical considerations are addressed.
weaknesses: The main evaluation is analytical and does not directly demonstrate that optimizing SRP or SCH leads to improved real expert-offloading throughput or memory savings; the only throughput-related evidence in Appendix F shows weak correlations with SCH.

SCH relies on an oracle with future activation-frequency information, and although it correlates with LRU/LFU hit rates, its practical achievable cache performance remains indirect and unvalidated with a realistic predictor.

Several central claims, such as shared experts harming routing consistency and domain-specialized experts contributing more than vocabulary-specialized ones, are supported mainly by correlational analyses and small-scale toy models; causal factors and confounders are not fully isolated.
SRP can be inflated by degenerate or highly imbalanced routing, and the supplementary size-ratio metric may not fully disentangle routing consistency from load imbalance in model-level comparisons.

The recommendation that cache size around 2x active experts balances effectiveness and efficiency appears overgeneralized: it is clearest for Group 1 models, while Groups 3 and 4 show near-linear SCH growth without a clear turning point.

Evaluation is limited to base models and fixed 512-token sequences in the main text; longer contexts, topic shifts, and post-trained model variants are only partially explored, which may affect offloading behavior.
